before.title: Cracking differential mount (studs rip out of the frame)
before.description: The diff is hung from the frame on a forward 'mustache' bracket and rear mounts. The forward differential mounting points are prone to cracking; the right-front point fails first because it carries the most torque load. As the mount works loose the crack propagates and, if ignored, the mounting studs eventually tear out of the frame, letting the diff move under power. The classic tell is a rear-end 'clunk' on sudden throttle application that starts intermittent and progresses to every power-on/off transition.
before.solution: If caught early you may only need fresh rubber diff mounting bushings, but the proven bulletproofing fix is a reinforcement kit: weld in a Moss/Sport Car Parts differential-mount repair kit that adds new studs, brackets and (on the front) reinforcing plates that spread the load and stop the crack from returning. The job is done with the diff out — grind out and weld up any existing crack, fit the reinforcing plate over the cross-member, install the new pin/studs, and renew the mount bushings at the same time. Polyurethane diff mount bushings are a common durability upgrade over the soft OEM rubber.
symptoms: Rear 'clunk' on sudden throttle on/off
Driveline shudder or movement when loading/unloading the drivetrain
Visible crack at the forward diff mount cross-member
Loose or pulled diff mounting studs
Worn/collapsed rubber diff mount bushings

before.title: Crankshaft thrust-washer wear and excessive end float
before.description: The straight-six uses semicircular (half-moon) crankshaft thrust washers at the centre main rather than full-circle thrusts, and the soft lead-indium face wears quickly. As they wear, crankshaft end float grows beyond the 0.006–0.008 in spec; past about 0.015 in the coating is gone and once the alloy wears through to steel it accelerates, scoring the crank thrust faces and eventually letting a washer drop into the sump. Riding the clutch at stoplights drives the wear hard. Worst case the crank walks fore-and-aft and destroys the block thrust faces — a full bottom-end job.
before.solution: Check end float with a dial indicator (lever the crank fore/aft) at every opportunity and especially after break-in; if it exceeds ~0.010–0.012 in, pull the centre main cap and fit oversize thrust washers to bring float back to 0.006–0.008 in. Restorers bulletproof this during a rebuild by fitting quality thrust washers and, on the best builds, having the bearing holder machined for bronze thrust washers/bushings instead of the original whitemetal. The cheapest insurance is the driving habit the community insists on: put the gearbox in neutral and release the clutch at stoplights instead of sitting with the pedal down.
symptoms: Measured end float over 0.008 in growing toward 0.015 in
Knock or fore-aft crank movement felt at the clutch
Metallic flakes/half-moon washer found in the sump
Crankshaft thrust face scoring on teardown
Low oil pressure / debris after break-in of a fresh rebuild

before.title: Lucas charging and electrical gremlins (corroded earths, weak alternator)
before.description: Like most British cars of the era the TR6 runs Lucas electrics with bullet-connector harnesses, a 16/17ACR alternator and lots of in-line earths through the body and bulb holders. Decades of corrosion at terminal blocks, the positive battery cable connections, the brown feed wires and the ignition-warning-light circuit (alternator brown/yellow + ignition white) cause flickering lights, no-charge faults, and a warning lamp that lies. Owners report that even a brand-new harness won't fix a charging fault when the real problem is a corroded earth or a tired regulator/alternator.
before.solution: Restorers cure it at the root: fit a quality reproduction wiring harness, then clean and protect every earth point (engine-to-frame and frame-to-body bonding straps added), and clean the brown feed wires and battery terminals. The popular bulletproofing upgrades are converting the points distributor to electronic ignition (Pertronix), and swapping the old 16ACR-style alternator for a modern higher-output internally-regulated alternator so the gauges and any added electric fan have reliable current. Note: with electronic ignition, never crank or run with a plug lead off — it can fry the module.
symptoms: Ignition/no-charge warning light glowing or flickering
Battery not charging despite a 'good' alternator test
Dim or intermittent lights and gauges
Voltage that drops with revs / wandering ammeter
Hard starting traced to corroded brown feed or earth connections

before.title: Lucas PI petrol-injection: hot-start failure, blocked injectors, fuel surge
before.description: European-market TR6 PI cars use the Lucas mechanical petrol-injection system, fed by a Lucas high-pressure pump. It is notoriously difficult to set up and live with: hard hot-starting after standing, blocked injectors, throttle-shaft wear that wrecks the mixture balance, and a pump/metering unit that ages poorly. Early TR5/TR6 PI tanks also lack an anti-surge reservoir, so on a tight left-hander below a quarter tank the engine fuel-starves and stumbles. This is the single most temperamental system on the car for a restorer.
before.solution: Two proven paths. Keep-it-original camp: rebuild the metering unit and injectors, replace worn throttle shafts, fit a modern Bosch high-pressure pump conversion kit (Revington TR) in place of the failure-prone original Lucas pump, and install a tank with the correct anti-surge reservoir to cure cornering starvation. Reliability-first camp: convert to twin Stromberg/SU or Weber carburettors (the US-spec setup) for far easier tuning and dependable starting, accepting a small power trade. Either way, address the anti-surge tank so the car doesn't cut out in corners.
symptoms: Won't restart when hot after standing
Rough idle and uneven full-throttle from throttle-shaft wear
Stumble/cut-out on left turns with under a quarter tank
Blocked injector causing a dead/weak cylinder
Failing Lucas high-pressure pump (noise, low pressure)

before.title: Marginal cooling / overheating in traffic and hot weather
before.description: The TR6's small 16 x 16.5 in radiator and engine-driven fan leave little cooling margin, so cars run hot idling in traffic and in hot climates, especially once the original brass core is partially silted up or the timing/mixture isn't right. The factory fan moves little air at idle, and a clogged or tired radiator pushes temperatures into the danger zone in stop-and-go driving.
before.solution: Bulletproof the system as a package rather than chasing one part: refresh the basics first (verify the thermostat opens, correct belt tension, healthy water pump, full flush) then fit an aluminum cross-flow/high-capacity radiator (Wizard Cooling, US Radiator) sized for the TR6, and add a thermostatically-switched electric cooling fan (e.g. Hayden/Spal ~14 in) which the community reports drops idle temps roughly 6–10°F and removes the parasitic drag of the engine fan. A 13-blade 'tropical' fan is the cheaper interim fix if staying engine-driven. Always confirm ignition timing and mixture, since a lean/retarded TR6 runs hot.
symptoms: Temperature climbing while idling or in slow traffic
Coolant loss / boiling over in hot weather
Runs cool on the move but heats up when stopped
Old/silted brass radiator core
Engine-driven fan moving little air at idle

before.title: Perished rear-suspension bushings causing rear camber/handling vagueness
before.description: The TR6's semi-trailing-arm independent rear suspension relies on soft rubber bushings at the trailing-arm pivots and fixed (non-adjustable) factory brackets. After decades the rubber perishes and collapses, letting rear camber and toe wander under load, which gives the car a vague, darty rear end, uneven inner-edge tyre wear, and clunks. The fixed factory bracket also can't correct the excessive negative camber a sagged car develops, and stresses the inner mount (a contributor to the trailing-arm bracket cracking restorers see).
before.solution: The standard bulletproofing rebuild is polyurethane trailing-arm bushings (SuperPro/Prothane) in place of the worn rubber for a firmly-planted rear without a harsh ride, combined with Goodparts/Richard Good adjustable trailing-arm brackets so rear camber can actually be set correctly instead of living with the factory's excess negative camber. Do it alongside fresh shocks/springs and a full inspection of the trailing-arm mounts, since the same area is the chassis crack/rust hot-spot. Properly set up, owners report flat, predictable cornering and even tyre wear.
symptoms: Vague or darty rear end under power and over bumps
Excessive negative rear camber / inner-edge tyre wear
Clunks from the rear trailing-arm pivots
Collapsed or cracked rubber trailing-arm bushings
Rear toe/camber that changes as the car is loaded
